Balochistan’s wounds. ALTHOUGH Balochistan has been experiencing varying degrees of tumult for over two decades now, currently, the troubled province is witnessing near-constant terrorist activity and lawlessness. The rulers in both Islamabad and Quetta often downplay the situation, but there are moments when they themselves admit that all is not well in Balochistan. For instance, on Friday, when the nation was celebrating Independence Day, the province’s Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti extended an olive branch to those engaged in violence. Mr Bugti advised the lawless elements to “return to the national mainstream” and talk to the government. However, he added, and rightly so, that the state would not talk to those who were involved in the killing of innocent people. In recent times, terrorist activity in Balochistan has become noticeably brazen. While ordinary citizens and security personnel are often targeted, even the high-level guardians of the state are not safe. On Friday, Balochistan Home Minister Ziaullah Langove’s convoy came under attack as he was returning to Quetta from Kalat. The minister survived the ambush, but a number of personnel who were accompanying him were wounded in the attack. Elsewhere, security forces have not yet given clearance for repair work on a gas pipeline that was blown up by the terrorists. The latter’s act of sabotage has deprived several towns of gas. While the chief minister has once again invited ‘angry’ elements for talks, the state has yet to create conducive conditions for dialogue to get off the ground. At this point, some introspection is required: the state has alienated even those political elements in Baloch society that have been peacefully pursuing their rights. This attitude must change. In the short term, a genuine process of reconciliation can begin by inviting both veteran Baloch politicians and younger activists to the table, and listening to their grievances. Questionable cases against peaceful activists should also be reviewed. If the state is able to build confidence through such measures, the next step can be taken to address long-term goals, such as ensuring that the people of Balochistan are given the first right to their province’s vast mineral wealth. The province’s miserable socioeconomic numbers also need the state’s immediate attention; this may take decades to fix, but the first step must be taken now. Claims that hostile foreign forces are stirring up trouble in Balochistan carry much weight. These forces must be exposed and kinetic action should continue against those involved in terrorism in Balochistan. But a long-term solution lies in taking the political path and involving the genuine representatives of the residents. The people will be waiting to see what practical steps the state takes to take forward the process of reconciliation in the province. Published in Dawn, August 16th, 2026

Makkah Agreement. THE Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Aug 7, stands out for one clause: an attack on any of the three countries is an attack on all. Coming in the wake of the recent tensions in the Middle East, this agreement has the potential to reshape the strategic layout of the region. Pakistan’s foreign ministry has described the agreement as a reflection of a “shared commitment” to further strengthen the “collective security” of the region. Understandably, the Makkah Agreement does not give the specifics of the commitments that each side has made. Such matters lie in the realm of operational details that are generally kept confidential. What is, however, clear is that it is not a military bloc. Nor is it aimed at any specific country. Since these three countries have different threat perceptions, the agreement seems to be an attempt to enhance their collective deterrence and defence capabilities to deal with any aggression. In the midst of the US-Iran tensions, Saudi Arabia came to the conclusion that the American security umbrella was not working. It started exploring multilayered security arrangements, including a strategic mutual defence agreement with Pakistan and a civil nuclear agreement with the US. In some ways, the Makkah Agreement is an upgrade on the existing Pak-Saudi defence agreement. Anchored in Turkiye’s defence manufacturing capabilities, Saudi Arabia’s financial heft and Pakistan’s trained forces and capabilities, as demonstrated in the war with India in May 2025 , the agreement marks an important strategic landmark in the evolution of a new security architecture of West Asia. Beyond the three countries’ deterrence and defence needs, there are regional and global aspects to discuss. Detractors are projecting it as an anti-Iran, Sunni group. The Turkish foreign minister has stated clearly that neither Iran nor anyone else was the target of this agreement. Iran’s spokesperson also indicated that Iran has no reason to fear the agreement, as regional countries, rather than outside powers, were working on regional security. Importantly, the Makkah Agreement ensures that there would be no single regional hegemon should America decide to retreat from the area. Given that the agreement is predicated on the idea of collective security, Iran and other countries in the neighbourhood could possibly join the agreement in due course so that a durable regional security architecture is established. The accord shouldn’t be seen as a military bloc. The Makkah Agreement is also a strong signal to Israel that its ambition of establishing Greater Israel and dominating the region is over. The US strategy to use the Abraham Accords to integrate Israel into Gulf security is also no longer plausible. The three signatories have consistently called upon Israel to stop its genocide of Palestinians in Gaza and respect international law and UN resolutions calling for an independent state of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. The accord reduces the US burden of protecting the Gulf states and places the region on the path of self-reliance through collective security. America has two vested interests in the region. One is Israel’s security. The second is the continuity of petro-dollars. The US-Iran war has shown the limits of Israeli regional dominance, while America will do its utmost to ensure that the pricing of oil remains in US dollars. The petro-dollar is increasingly likely to be challenged by several countries desiring to buy Iranian and other oil in non-dollar currencies. Yet, it is important for the three signatories to take the US on boa­rd on the scope of this agreement. As for China, it will be pleased with the ag­­reement as it helps expand its concept of collective security encapsulated in the Global Security Initiative. As it is, any step that seems to weaken America’s footprint in the region is a welcome development in Chinese and Russian eyes. Pakistan’s leadership has done well by consistently using its peace diplomacy to not only bring stability to the region but also shape an entirely new image of the country. At the same time, Pakistan must continue its constructive engagement with Iran and major powers. While these strategic alignments serve the interests of the three signatories and the region, it would be useful to explore a corresponding initiative of concluding a trilateral economic agreement to pool together resources for the shared interests of the three states. The ultimate message of the Makkah Agreement is that the region is secure only when every country located in it is safe and when a culture of cooperation replaces one of confrontation. It is also clear that diplomacy backed by credible defence capabilities is the best guard against kinetic misadventures. The writer is former foreign secretary and chairman of Sanober Institute. Published in Dawn, August 16th, 2026

Endless wait for a miracle. PAKISTAN celebrated its 79th Independence Day a couple of days ago. Once again, the anniversary arrived wrapped in the optimism that perhaps the next year will be different and bring some relief to ordinary citizens. The source of this optimism is the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement . Walls have been covered with graffiti, while stre­ets have been decorated with buntings, flags and pictures of the leaders of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. Pakistan’s streets witnessed similar enthusiasm just over a decade ago, when the country’s power elites sold the nation the dream of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor ( CPEC ). Though the Makkah Agreement is different from CPEC in essence, as the latter project was conceived as a plan for economic connectivity, the recent trilateral accord is a geopolitical initiative involving the region’s middle powers, and ordinary people have attached their hopes to it. Just as they expected CPEC to bring relief to their lives, create employment and generate economic activity, the perception now being nurtured is that the accord will bring foreign investment into the country, Saudi money, oil on deferred payments and employment for more Pakistanis in the Gulf. Waiting for a miracle to happen is an old practice of Pakistan’s power elite. Every few years, the ruling establishment constructs a new narrative of hope: that a breakthrough is just around the corner, prosperity is waiting beyond the horizon, and Pakistan need only remain patient for the miracle to unfold. This habit of looking abroad for transformation dates back to the country’s inception, when its leadership placed its hopes in the US, joined Seato and Cento, and became a Western defence and security partner alongside Iran. Pakistan’s dreams of geopolitical influence and economic gains through its defence partnership with the US have been shattered repeatedly. Yet, its power elites have repeatedly restored their optimism and embraced new partnerships, expecting external allies to increase the country’s strategic weight and generate financial inflows. The same pattern has extended from Pakistan’s relationship with the US and its Western alliances to its strategic partnership with China, the CPEC, the anticipated opening of Central Asia, and now, the emerging security architecture involving Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. One may recall that when Nawaz Sharif began his third term as prime minister in 2013, and CPEC was formally launched in 2015, it was described as a ‘ game changer ’. Islamabad’s streets were covered with Pakistani and Chinese flags, creating the impression that an extraordinary partnership was about to transform Pakistan’s economic destiny. China and Pakistan were and remain close strategic partners, and CPEC has delivered important infrastructure and energy projects. But more than a decade after its launch, the promised transformation remains incomplete. Pakistan continues to struggle with debt, inadequate exports , weak productivity and recurring balance-of-payments crises. It still depends on IMF programmes, financial deposits, loan rollovers and other forms of support from friendly countries, including China and Saudi Arabia. CPEC therefore demonstrates the limits of relying on external partnerships as substitutes for the difficult domestic reforms required for sustained economic transformation. Pakistanis have been conditioned to look outward for a change in their fate. In the same sequence, the power elites cultivated the dream of economic transformation through Afghanistan. When the Taliban came to power , Pakistan’s dreams of connecting economically and strategically with Central Asia and regions beyond would come true. One may recall Independence Day in 2021, when the power elites were echoing similar narratives about Afghanistan. As the Taliban approached Kabul, flags of the Islamic emirate appeared at some mosques and other locations in Islamabad. The Taliban entered the Afghan capital on Aug 15, a day after Pakistan celebrated its Independence Day. The mood in influential Pakistani circles was strikingly jubilant. The prime minister at the time, Imran Khan, remarked that Afghans had broken the “ shackles of slavery ”. Pakistan became one of the strongest advocates of international engagement with the new Taliban administration, although it stopped short of granting formal recognition. At a public seminar, I heard a retired security official confidently predict that the Taliban’s victory would trigger a profound social and political transformation inside Pakistan. He argued that the new order in Afghanistan would eliminate corruption and inspire a more just system in Pakistan. He carefully avoided using the word ‘Sharia’, perhaps because of his professional background, but his meaning was difficult to miss. It was another utopian moment. The reality moved in the opposite direction. Afghanistan’s economic and humanitarian crisis produced new displacement, while the banned TTP intensified its attacks. Relations between Islamabad and Kabul deteriorated sharply. Instead of facilitating regional connectivity, insecurity across the border became one of Pakistan’s gravest internal threats. That episode has been recounted many times, although the security establishment now appears reluctant to revisit the assumptions that shaped its initial enthusiasm. The latest defence pact has sparked another wave of optimism. It may indeed strengthen Pakistan’s strategic position. Its significance should therefore be assessed realistically rather than burdened with promises it may never have been designed to fulfil. Partners and projects change, but the underlying psychology remains remarkably constant. Pakistanis have been conditioned to look outward for a change in their fate. The internal front, however, remains far more complex and generates little optimism. Reforming institutions is more difficult than signing agreements. Building political consensus is less dramatic than receiving a foreign dignitary. Improving governance does not produce the spectacle of flags lining Islamabad’s avenues. One wishes an Independence Day would come when our optimism is the result of something Pakistan had achieved at home: an economic transformation initiated by our own policies; functioning institutions; sustainable peace in Balochistan; stable relationships with Afghanistan and India; the elimination of all insecurities; the rule of law; and, above all, the return of true democracy. Perhaps it is human nature for individuals and nations caught in a crisis to search outside themselves for rescue. Pakistan suffers from the same temptation. Every few years, it discovers another reason to be jubilant, another alliance and another reason to wait for the miracle. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, August 16th, 2026

SMOKERS’ CORNER: POLITICS OF THE BIG TENT. In Europe and the United States, the post-1945 era marked a shift from ‘mass parties’ to broad ‘big-tent’ parties. Mass parties had operated on strict class lines. Democratic socialist outfits appealed to industrial workers, while conservative parties represented business elites and religious traditionalists. Big-tent politics had already taken root in North America due to its vast geography, rapid industrialisation, and diverse immigrant and Black populations. To build winning national majorities, the Democratic and Republican parties developed broad platforms, accommodating competing internal factions under a shared umbrella and a loose ideological core. This was the beginning of big-tent parties. The Democratic Party in the US, especially from the early 1930s onwards, has housed democratic socialists, progressives, social liberals and pro-business centrists, alongside its conservative Southern wing, which existed within the party till the early 1960s. The latter was mainly to bag votes from the ‘Bible belt’ states. The modern Republican Party functions as a broad umbrella encompassing social conservatives, Christian nationalists, fiscal centrists and right-wing populists. A similar evolution occurred in western Europe after World War II. According to the German jurist Otto Kirchheimer, as the post-war economic growth expanded the middle-class, most voters began to favour pragmatic moderation over class antagonism. Left-wing parties, such as the UK Labour Party and Germany’s Social Democratic Party, shifted toward a progressive centre-left stance, while centre-right parties, such as the British Conservatives and Germany’s Christian Democrats, softened their hard social moralism and elitism to capture votes from across the classes. Political scientists mostly view big-tent parties as important democratic stabilisers. By absorbing diverse economic, regional and social groups, a big-tent outfit facilitates them to negotiate and form a consensus under a single umbrella. This prevents extreme polarisation and avoids the chaotic parliamentary fragmentation typical of unstable multiparty systems that lack big-tent parties. From the Democrats and Republicans in the United States to the PPP, PML-N and PTI in Pakistan, the very diversity that makes big-tent parties electorally powerful can also become their greatest vulnerability Big-tent outfits combine diverse demands and elements, transforming societal rivalries into organised, workable governing units. The success of a big-tent party depends on how they design mechanisms to manage internal dissent. Rather than enforcing monolithic obedience, party structures use primary elections, regional quotas and factional appointments to give diverse interest groups a seat at tables that matter. This internal diplomacy allows the overarching party to remain flexible. A well-managed big-tent party can position its platform across different political cycles, moving slightly leftward or rightward to keep pace with changing electorate moods, without suffering an electoral decline. Following the 1947 Partition , India saw a classic big-tent system emerge under the Indian National Congress (INC). Operating on a secular, centre-left platform, Congress absorbed diverse socialist, moderate and regional groups to maintain a 30-year political monopoly. As the nation’s founding party, it offered a shared national brand that co-opted multiple local political elites and bridged vast linguistic and religious divides. INC’s dominance was broken in 1977 by the Janata Party (JP). JP was a broad anti-INC coalition of secular, regional, Hindutva and left-wing groups who couldn’t find a place under INC’s tent. However, JP illustrated a common pitfall related to big-tent politics: unmanaged factional infighting. Driven by intense ideological friction and personal rivalries among its leadership, JP collapsed from within after just three years in power. When internal fractures widen in big-tent parties, the parties tend to lose their electoral appeal or fall prey to radical internal takeovers. This occurred within the US Republican Party, where the right-wing populist Maga (Make America Great Again) movement led by Donald Trump weaponised primary elections to displace the Republican Party’s dominant free market and moderate factions. The populist wing of the party then reoriented the outfit into becoming a nationalist-populist vehicle. But this transformation has introduced severe vulnerabilities, driven by infighting within the party’s populist wing, foreign policy controversies and an increasing backlash in the US against Israeli lobby groups such as the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). Trump’s approval ratings have plummeted . The Democrats are facing their own internal tensions. Key primary victories by progressive candidates of the party have alarmed its centrist factions, who fear left-leaning Democrats could alienate moderate voters in upcoming national contests. In South Asia, apart from INC and then JP, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) began to function as a big-tent party. Historically a Hindu nationalist party with an upper-caste base, the BJP began to widen its umbrella. It started to accommodate distinct groups: Hindutva hardliners, big business groups, populists and pragmatists absorbed from opposition parties. Hindutva remains the BJP’s ideological anchor, though, even as it increasingly applies big-tent electoral strategies. Pakistan developed a big-tent model led by the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) and the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N). Before these, Pakistan’s founding party, the Muslim League, had successfully managed to combine a wide range of left to right groups to win enough seats in the 1946 elections in British India, which allowed it to push for a separate Muslim-majority country. But after the creation of Pakistan, friction between different groups in the League became so intense that the party fractured. The PPP, formed in 1967, shaped a centre-left core with diverse leftist, progressive, liberal and centrist groups, while the PML-N, formed in 1992, united urban pro-business cohorts, landed elites, centrists and social conservatives. In 2011, facilitated by the then military establishment, the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) expanded into a third big-tent party by absorbing traditional ‘electables’ from the two existing big-tent outfits. PTI operated as an archetypal contemporary populist party, weaving a flexible and performative core of right- and left-wing tropes around a central anti-corruption narrative and personal loyalty to its leader. This vague ideological architecture allowed urban middle-class youth, conservatives, landed elites and mainstream Islamists to coexist under one banner. However, like India’s Janata Party, PTI struggled to manage its internal frictions and rapidly unravelled once its top leader was removed from power and imprisoned. Big-tent parties remain double-edged constructs. While their capacity to combine diverse interests and build broad platforms shields democracies against fragmentation, their reliance on a conflicted ideological core and mismanaged internal conflicts leaves them vulnerable. This requires continuous maintenance. Without disciplined leadership, big-tent parties risk devolving into factional warfare, opening the door to radical takeovers or collapse when internal consensus breaks down. Maintaining a workable equilibrium remains a constant challenge. In Pakistan, big-tent parties such as the PML-N and the PPP have done remarkably well to avoid disintegration despite attempts by previous military establishments to dismantle them by exploiting their internal frictions. This ability to regroup and survive is something that PTI has, so far, failed to demonstrate. Published in Dawn, EOS, August 16th, 2026

Rampant Bangladesh make history with first-ever Test win in Australia. A dominant Bangladesh stunned hosts Australia to win the first Test by nine wickets in Darwin on Sunday for a historic maiden Test victory on Australian soil. After bowling Australia out for 284 and needing 57 to win, the visitors cruised past the total when Mominul Haque slashed Beau Webster to the backward point boundary. Bangladesh dominated Australia throughout the match and the margin of victory will send shockwaves through the cricketing world. After bowling Australia out for 198 in the first innings, the visitors always looked the more likely to win. They kept the pressure on throughout Sunday and didn’t panic when Cameron Green (104) brought up his third Test century after lunch on day four. Green was offered no real support from his teammates and the Bangladeshis kept taking vital scalps to leave Australia on the ropes, with Mehidy Hasan Miraz taking 5-66. The visitors went into the match with most observers giving them no chance of winning. Their only warm-up game, against a Cricket Australia XI, ended in a big loss that included a second-innings collapse where they were all out for 54. But they have completely outplayed the Australians and won every session, batting, bowling and catching better than their more illustrious counterparts. Australia, fielding their best possible team, have looked out of sorts from the beginning. Their batting failed in the first innings when they were bowled out on the opening day, then their much-vaunted bowling attack struggled against the gritty Bangladesh batsmen. Led by a maiden Test century from opener Tanzid Hasan , Bangladesh made 426 and importantly kept Australia in the field for 138 overs in Darwin’s heat and humidity. The bowlers then showed great patience Saturday to make regular breakthroughs and keep Australia under the cosh. When Australia resumed Sunday on 161-4, most of their hopes lay with Alex Carey and Green. Carey lived dangerously in the opening 30 minutes, twice edging seamer Hasan Mahmud through the vacant slips cordon for boundaries. But on 30 Mehidy produced a beautiful ball, pitching in line then turning sharply to take Carey’s outside edge to wicketkeeper Litton Das. He struck again soon after, bowling Webster for five to leave Australia 193-6 and in deep trouble. A famous victory edged ever closer when Australia captain Pat Cummins pushed forward to a Mehidy delivery and got an inside edge to short leg, where Shadman Islam took a sharp chance. Australia were 207-7, still 21 runs behind Bangladesh’s first-innings total. Green and Mitchell Starc batted sensibly to ensure Bangladesh had to bat again. Starc fell for 18 caught behind but Green was playing well and brought up his century shortly after lunch. But despite looking increasingly comfortable, he was undone when a Hasan ball kept low, hit the toe end of his bat and cannoned into the stumps. Mehidy wrapped up the innings when he trapped Nathan Lyon plumb in front leg before. Depsite losing Tanzid in the first over, Mominul and Shadman Islam cruised to victory.

Banking today: Digital connectivity and accessibility. HEARD IT THROUGH THE GRIPE-VINE The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Circular 1238 took effect on July 4, 2026; with the core rule of requiring fair, transparent, and cost-based market pricing for electronic fund transfers. And while the Bangko Sentral was not forcing financial institutions, from traditional banks to electronic money issuers and e-wallets, to offer zero fees; the principle of fair pricing was hailed across the board, by FinTech Alliance PH, and especially by micro-merchants. As a result of the Circular, fees for cross institution and interbank fund transfers do not materially differ from same bank, same wallet transfers. This may be well and good; but the question for me was how does this affect us, the regular financial institution client, and the public at large? So I approached one of the banks I deal with regularly, EastWest, to gain some enlightenment; to appreciate how this could fit under, and extend, their cornerstone advocacy of Digital adaptation and transformation. Let’s first define some terms - as I find Filipinos are notoriously shy to ask for clarification, often resorting to the nodding of one’s head to imply comprehension, even if they have only a limited grasp of what’s being said. First, there’s Digitization - which is merely converting physical records into digital files, to PDFs and MP3s. Then there’s Digitalization- defined as the leveraging of data to improve and automate processes. And most important for us in today’s column, there’s digital adaptation and transformation - this refers to a cultural and operational overhaul, altering how business operates and delivers value to the customers. If the first two concepts are more inward-looking, within a company or banking institution; the third involves looking outward, recasting the interaction with its customers. EastWest (EW) promotes digital adaptation; integrating digital technology in workflow, business models, and culture - in short, in its’ everyday life. EW delivers value, responds to market shifts, and protects against cybersecurity threats; balancing technology upgrades with organizational capability, development, and risk management. It’s core focus areas are automation, data driven decision making (the shift to analytics), workforce readiness, security, and resilience. I like how Filinvest Group director and EastWest Bank FVP and Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer Isabelle Gotianun Yap expounded on this, starting with the top view from Filinvest, then defining it for their banking arm, East West; “At Filinvest, innovation begins with understanding what people and businesses genuinely need. We look beyond the technology itself, and focus on how it can make everyday experiences easier, and more valuable to the communities we serve.” “When we look at data such as EastWest’s 53.26 percent digital penetration rate, and about 1.36 million digital users, as of end April 2026, it is important to remember that these numbers represent real people and customers. Behind every transaction or interaction is someone looking for a simpler, more convenient way to manage their banking needs.” It’s giving digital adaptation the human face it needs. EastWest brings this to life by creating multiple touch points for this digital adaptation to take root. The guiding principle is to seamlessly adapt, so it fits with your lifestyle. For retail customers, the EasyWay mobile app makes it convenient to manage accounts, transfer funds, and pay bills anytime and anywhere. For business owners, cash flow management and payments can be done through EasyBiz, via a web browser. Meanwhile, KOMO mobile app offers high-interest savings accounts, and provides access to products such as the Teacher’s salary loan. EastWest makes payments easier with its growing digital payment ecosystem. If one is an EW credit card holder, EastWest Pay allows one to leave the physical card at home, and still have full use of the card when one is out. For an everyday smartphone user, it’s GooglePay. Your EW VISA debit or credit card, or EW Mastercard credit card, can be added to your Google Wallet, and then ‘hop on’ to GooglePay. It’s accepted globally, and can be used with compatible smartwatches and wearables. And for those with an active lifestyle, EW went the further mile and became Garmin Pay’s online traditional bank partner. So you can run, swim, cycle, play sports; and if you have your Garmin device on your wrist, you’re good to make payments at that coffee stop, snack bar, or supermarket. EW is also leveraging AI. ESTA (EastWest System Tech Assistant) is the bank’s AI-powered digital assistant, allowing users to get information, and perform a range of credit card services. The bank also launched ECHO, or EW CMS Help Officer, an AI-powered chatbot designed to help business owners better understand, and access EW’s cash management services. EastWest and their drive for Digital Adaptation is about enhancing connectivity and accessibility, embedding digital engagement in our everyday life. With digital payments already accounting for 57.4 percent of retail transactions in our country, its clearly about leading this Transformation, or being left in the dust.

Arun Gogna, the happy preacher. ENDEAVOR While browsing on Facebook last week, my attention was caught by a series of reels featuring Arun Gogna, a highly engaging preacher who, I realized was, like me, a Bosconian from Don Bosco Makati. Arun’s style is light and breezy. His main pitch is easy to recall. We need to have a personal relationship with God. Jesus our Savior is merciful and overflows with love for each of us. In every step we make, God touches our lives and makes it meaningful. He is married to Dr. Lallaine Lucas-Gogna, an orthodontist. The couple lives in Parañaque, Metro Manila, with their two children, a daughter named Andrea Helene and a son named Yohan Gabriel. After many years of working together as co-preachers, Bo Sanchez stepped aside and tapped Arun to assume leadership of The Feast community. Here are excerpts from his poignant note: “Arun, thank you for the sacrifice of accepting the burden of shepherding God's people. You bravely took over my leadership role two years ago and made my happy retirement possible. For this, I'll always be grateful. You're leading so much better than me, I should have passed on my leadership many years ago. It's an honor serving with you and doing life together.” Indeed, Arun has gone a long way from the start of his ministry in a parish charismatic community. He relates: “We organized the top leaders from the Light of Jesus Family chapters of Alabang, Parañaque, Las Pinas, Muntinlupa, and Laguna.” The formation of the servant leaders and their teams ensued. Aside from discipleship, their focal points of attention were finance, production and marketing. Prayer and faith were the building blocks. Arun recalls holding a Jericho Pray-Over of the leaders on top of a building, and responding to the needs of an ever-growing community. Today, Arun’s community converges at the Bellevue hotel and the Festival Mall in Alabang. Let me share with you a sampler of his memorable reels. There’s a real-life vignette between a father and a son entitled Loving God with Everything from Arun’s book entitled Happy Secrets to an Obedient Life. Arun narrates how a teen-age boy sought and obtained permission from his dad to attend a dance party with friends. The young lad promised to come home at one o’clock in the morning. But he must have enjoyed the company very much as he stayed out past his self-imposed curfew, before deciding to head home at 3 a.m. To his chagrin, the front door was locked. But a few moments later, it was opened by his dad. Instead of scolding him, his dad laid out a mat and two pillows for them to sleep over at the doorstep of their home. By such act of compassion toward his son, the father was emulating the Lord of Divine Mercy’s humility. A gifted communicator, Arun uses simple tools to convey key messages. For instance, he used a rope to illustrate the ways in which parents guide their children through different stages of maturity. Wearing a controller’s hat, parents permit their children to socialize and develop bonds of fellowship and trust with friends during their teenage years. When the children finish college and start working, the degrees and scope of freedom that they enjoy are increased. At this point, their parents wear a new headgear, the coaching hat. They tell their children about the implications of eventually choosing lifetime partners. Arun assures parents: “Babalik din sila at mamahalin kayo.” (Your children will come back and reaffirm their love for you.) The key lesson is this: the only way to hold on to your children is to let them go, trusting that God will guide them and keep them in the right path. In another reel, Arun walked down memory lane and recalled his wedding to his erstwhile girlfriend Lallaine. “Nung pinapanood ko yung magiging asawa ko na magmamartsa patungo sa altar, tinanong ko ang aking sarili: Bakit kaya niya ako nagustuhan at pinili? (While watching my wife-to-be marching down the aisle, I asked myself: Why did she like and choose me to be her husband?) “I realized then that I did not define her by her weaknesses; I defined her as the person I have loved for four years and will continue to love forever.” Above all, Preacher Arun counsels the flock: Trust in the Lord Jesus and repose your faith in the Almighty, for He gives rest to the weary, solace to the aggrieved, mercy to those seeking forgiveness. Indeed, it’s pure joy to watch and learn from Arun Gogna, the happy preacher. Comments may be sent to sonnycoloma@gmail.com

Eala-Ruse match delayed by inclement weather. Alex Eala’s second round match against Romanian Elena-Gabriela Ruse in the WTA1000 Cincinnati Open has been suspended due to an approaching inclement weather and lightning threat in the wee hours of Sunday, Aug. 16 (Manila time) Dark and thick clouds blanketed the skies over the Lindner Family Tennis Center, prompting officials to temporarily stop the play with Eala comfortably ahead, 6-1, 3-0. “ Play has been suspended due to inclement weather approaching. Please seek shelter,” said Cincinnati Open on its official X account. As of press time, there’s no official word yet when the match will resume. Earlier, the contest was also briefly halted after a fan collapsed on the bleachers amid humid weather conditions. Ruse also called a medical timeout prior to the pause to address what appeared to be a right foot injury.

The luxury of coming home at Shang Residences Wack Wack. Urban luxury living has evolved into something deeply personal. It is no longer just about square meterage or high-end finishes. Today, it is about the seamless integration of an expansive outward-facing panorama with a restorative, grounded inward environment. Having spent nearly two decades immersed in interior design, my definition of true luxury always circles back to a delicate equilibrium: the ability to retreat into absolute, intimate privacy while remaining connected to a vibrant, engaging world just beyond your glass. Among the residential towers I have stepped into, studied, or designed for over the years, Shang Residences Wack Wack—brought to life by renowned design studios Wong Tung and Partners, Asya Design, and BTR International—masterfully achieves this exact balance. Tucked just far enough from Metro Manila’s relentless commercial pace, this property reminds us that true luxury is, above all, a sense of sanctuary. It leverages its prized location to frame astounding vistas of the eastern horizon, offering tranquil, unobstructed views over the historic expanse of the Wack Wack Golf and Country Club. These panoramic views do far more than just please the eye as they anchor the home's emotional core. In spaces like these, thoughtful planning is everything. The layouts balance solitary respite with dynamic, spacious living zones, delivering absolute intimacy without ever making you feel closed off from the world outside. For me, the mark of a truly great development is when the design conversation doesn’t end at your front door, but flows seamlessly into the rhythm of the shared spaces. At Shang Residences Wack Wack, resort-style living is interpreted through rich, tactile layers: woven organic elements in wall claddings, soft fabric upholsteries, grounding natural stones, warm bronze metals, and artisanal earthenware. It is also refreshing to see furniture, decor, and art curated in a way that champions local Filipino talent on a global scale. Walking through the lobbies, hallways, and amenities, I find myself naturally looking at the details that casual visitors might miss. I am consistently struck by the meticulous attention paid to every surface—from the floors beneath to the ceilings overhead, right down to the subtle acoustic atmosphere of the grand lobby. These are hallmarks of genuine craftsmanship with refined transit zones featuring warm, cohesive material palettes, meticulous groove details, and thoughtful termination points that allow different materials to meet without friction. Layer in the resort-grade amenities—from a distinct fully equipped gym and wellness spaces like the steam room and sauna to the expansive outdoor pool—and you have an environment where wellness and community flow effortlessly into one another. At first glance, one might wonder if true privacy and vibrant urban living can ever truly coexist, or if we are always forced to choose between one or the other. But spending time within the architecture and interiors of the property erases that doubt. It is a rare find in the city—one that brilliantly marries an expansive outward horizon with the comforting, quiet intimacy of a private sanctuary.

Alex Eala off to a flyer in Cincinnati Open as Ruse retires. Alex Eala was off to a rousing start in the WTA 1000 Cincinnati Open, dominating Elena-Gabriela Ruse, 6-1, 3-0, before the Romanian retired in their rain-delayed second-round match early Sunday, Aug. 16 (Manila time). Save for an early hiccup that saw Eala drop her serve in the opening game, the Filipina tennis ace controlled the match before Ruse was forced to retire with an injury in the second set, following an hour-long delay due to inclement weather. The 17th-seeded Eala, armed with her blazing forehand and tricky lefty serve, overcame a slow start in the opening set before finding her rhythm and rattling off the next six games to draw first blood in the match. The 21-year-old Filipina kept her foot on the gas pedal and raced to a 3-0 lead before Ruse called for a medical timeout to attend to her right-foot injury. Play was subsequently delayed by rain and lightning, and the Romanian decided to not anymore continue, handing Eala a spot in the third round. She now sets up a Round of 32 showdown with American ninth seed Amanda Anisimova, who previously defeated Eala’s Turkish friend Zeynep Sonmez, 6-2, 6-3. The victory was some sort of revenge for Eala, who fell to Ruse in their first meeting in the third qualifying round of the 2024 Australian Open. The Filipino is also looking to bounce back from a fourth round exit in the Canadian Open.

Maria Gan marks her atelier’s first anniversary with a sampaguita-inspired bridal collection. Sampaguitas bring back many memories for me. I always look forward to buying a few garlands outside church, offering them, and keeping some blooms at home. I love their soft, delicate, and memorable fragrance. The scent brings to mind prayer, family traditions, and expressions of faith. It is fitting that our national flower represents purity, devotion, and love. For fashion designer Maria Gan, these qualities provided the starting point for “Sumpa, A Bridal Ode to Sampaguita,” her latest eight-piece collection. Presented during the first anniversary celebration of the Maria Gan Couture atelier on Aug. 8, it offers looks for every part of the wedding, from the preparations and ceremony to the reception and after-party. Instead of interpreting the flower literally, Maria drew inspiration from its qualities. “I wanted to capture its essence, its softness, intimacy, and symbolism of quiet devotion,” she tells Manila Bulletin Lifestyle. “This translated into silhouettes that feel like unfolding petals: gentle draping, curved lines, and sculpted forms that hold structure while remaining light.” Silk, Mikado, organdy, and duchess satin bring together delicacy and strength. Hand-appliquéd florals, cut-out motifs, and subtle beading appear throughout the collection. “It’s more about evoking a feeling than recreating the flower itself,” she says. From ceremony to after-party Each look was designed for a different part of the wedding celebration. Structured gowns in off-white and pearl tones offer classic options for the ceremony, while lighter pieces with sheer layers allow a bride to move more freely during the reception. Short dresses and separates provide contemporary choices for welcome dinners, after-parties, or smaller celebrations. “Alon,” a tiered dress with a fluid silhouette, may be worn for a pre-wedding event. “Giliw” can serve as a wedding preparation look or welcome dinner dress, while “Mutya” and “Sinta” present bridal separates for someone looking for a less traditional ensemble. “Tala” can be worn as a reception dress or for a beach wedding. “Hiraya” and “Wagas” are Maria’s interpretations of the classic bride, featuring the clean, cosmopolitan lines associated with her work. The collection’s namesake, “Sumpa,” carries its most personal detail: an overlay embroidered with a vow. Brides may request their own vows, initials, dates, lyrics, or meaningful phrases. These can be embroidered by hand or, if the bride would like the message to resemble her handwriting more closely, through machine embroidery. Personalization may take a few weeks, depending on the length and intricacy. “It becomes something intimate, worn close to the body. It’s a very intentional process, each word stitched with care, much like the garlands that inspired the collection,” says Maria. Made to be worn again Although bridal clothes are traditionally created for one important day, Maria considered how the pieces could remain in a woman’s wardrobe afterward. Tops may be worn with trousers, while skirts can be paired with other pieces. “Versatility was very important to me,” she says. “Many pieces can be restyled so they can live beyond the wedding day rather than existing as a single-use garment.” This responds to what Maria has observed during the atelier’s first year. Brides are becoming less focused on grandeur and more interested in meaning, comfort, and versatility. They are also more open to cleaner lines, lighter fabrics, and pieces they can wear again. The collection makes room for the traditional bride who values timeless elegance, the romantic drawn to softness and floral details, and the contemporary woman who prefers shorter hemlines, separates, or an unexpected silhouette. One year at the atelier The anniversary marks a new chapter for Maria, who has spent the past year gaining a better understanding of her clients and becoming more certain of her design identity. “I’ve learned to trust my intuition more. I realized over time that there is strength in creating intentional and personal pieces.” That confidence can be seen in a collection where the focus remains on cut, movement, fabric, and details carrying personal significance. For Maria, bridal wear brings together memory, identity, and change. “Designing for these moments is not just about creating something beautiful, but about creating something that holds meaning. It’s a privilege to be part of such an important chapter in someone’s life.”

Kids Around opens first Manila store at Greenbelt 5 with Chloé, Givenchy, Kenzo, and Boss. Children today are fortunate to have so many choices when it comes to what they wear. From classic pieces and playful prints to sporty looks and miniature versions of grown-up favorites, there is plenty of room for them to develop their own sense of style. Parents also get to have a little fun with it, especially when they can share some of the same fashion favorites with their mini-mes. The best part may be seeing children begin to make those choices themselves—the color they always reach for, the dress they insist on wearing, or the pair of sneakers that somehow goes with everything. Kids Around, a Paris-born premium and luxury childrenswear destination, is giving Filipino families even more options with the opening of its first Manila store at Greenbelt 5 in Makati City. The boutique brings Chloé, Givenchy, Kenzo, and Boss childrenswear together with Kids Around’s own label. Present in 29 countries with more than 85 boutiques, it carries clothing, shoes, and accessories for babies, children, and teenagers. “It is the first multi-brand concept store dedicated to children, so we house different designer brands,” Sabrina Miranda, group general manager of Adrenaline Group, the local operator of Kids Around, tells Manila Bulletin Lifestyle. “We want to let children explore, be curious, and find their own sense of style.” A little piece of Paris Inspired by Haussmannian architecture, the store interiors are designed to resemble a contemporary Parisian apartment, with light paneled walls, herringbone-style flooring, and touches of color. There are dedicated areas for girls, boys, babies, shoes, and accessories, making it easy for parents and children to look through the different collections together. Sabrina describes Givenchy as a choice for children who prefer a more urban, street-inspired style. Boss offers the classic “mini-me” look, including pieces for fathers who want their little ones dressed like them. Chloé has a softer, more relaxed and bohemian feel, while Kenzo is bright and playful. “We’re opening with these four brands. We also have our very own Kids Around label,” adds Sabrina. The latter brings in summery pieces, tennis prints, and bright yellows and greens, with designs inspired by vintage sportswear and the French Riviera. Something for every style For Spring/Summer 2026, Chloé Childrenswear goes romantic with pastels, sunset prints, florals, embroidery, ruffles, and lace. There are airy dresses and relaxed denim, along with shoes and accessories for those who like the fashion house’s signature feminine look in smaller sizes. Givenchy takes a more urban direction, mixing casual pieces with the polished Parisian style associated with the house. Kenzo Kids brings plenty of color, with references to Parisian and Japanese gardens appearing through peonies, elephants, and playful graphics inspired by sweets. Boss Kidswear looks to New York, Massachusetts, and Mexico City for its “The World Is Yours” collection. Graphic shirts, lightweight tailoring, sporty separates, and summer accessories carry the brand’s familiar clean look. This season, its mini-me concept also includes infants for the first time. Together, the labels give young shoppers very different wardrobes to choose from, whether they gravitate toward Kenzo’s colorful graphics, Chloé’s feminine details, Givenchy’s street style, or the more classic appeal of Boss. Bringing the brands together For Hans Yao, president of Adrenaline Group, having the different labels in one place is part of the appeal. He also has a personal fondness for the Parisian influence. “In our family, we like things that are French because they have that luxurious feel.” Greenbelt 5 will not be the only place to find the concept. Hans revealed that Adrenaline Group is also opening Kids Around at Rustan’s later this year. Marc Jacobs, Calvin Klein, and Karl Lagerfeld Kids are also part of the group’s childrenswear portfolio. For families who enjoy fashion, Kids Around makes shopping for children a little more interesting. Parents can introduce them to favorite labels, find those irresistible mini-me looks, and, at the same time, see which colors, prints, and styles their children choose for themselves. Sabrina sums it up, “We want to create an experience that celebrates children’s individuality and gives kids the freedom to discover their own sense of style.”

Gov’t to boost funding, support for LGUs — Recto. Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said the Marcos administration will continue increasing funding and direct support for local government units (LGUs) to help them deliver services more quickly to their constituents. Recto made the commitment after receiving the Presidential Action Agenda of the League of Municipalities of the Philippines (LMP) during the LMP Mindanao Island Cluster Conference in Cebu City on Aug. 13. He said the National Tax Allotment (NTA) of LGUs is expected to reach nearly PHP 1.4 trillion in 2027, the largest allocation in the country's history. “Halos 30 percent ng lahat ng koleksyon ng buwis ng pamahalaan ay awtomatikong ibinababa sa ating mga lokal na pamahalaan (Nearly 30 percent of all government tax collections are automatically allocated to our local governments),” Recto noted. “Ito ang pinakamalaking pondong direktang mapupunta sa mga LGU sa kasaysayan ng bansa (This is the largest fund that will directly go to LGUs in the country's history),” he said. The largest share of the NTA will go to 1,491 municipalities, which are set to receive a combined P448.70 billion, while 83 provinces will receive P303.56 billion, 149 cities will get P303.56 billion, and 41,912 barangays nationwide will receive P263.97 billion under the 2027 distribution. Aside from the NTA, Recto said the administration will further strengthen the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), which finances programs and projects identified as priorities in local communities. The proposed 2027 national budget includes P58.53 billion for the LGSF, which Recto described as the highest level in the fund's history. “Hindi namin gustong diktahan ang mga LGU kung ano ang dapat gawin (We do not want to dictate to LGUs what they should do),” he said. “Ang gusto namin ay makinig sa inyo, makipagtulungan sa inyo, at maghatid ng resulta kasama ninyo (We want to listen to you, work with you, and deliver results with you),” he added. Among the initiatives supported by the LGSF is the distribution of 10 kilograms of free rice every two months to nearly eight million Filipino families, as well as projects involving roads, farm-to-market roads, water systems, health facilities, and multipurpose buildings that can serve as evacuation centers during disasters. Recto said the government has also simplified the process for requesting LGSF assistance by reducing requirements and speeding up the release of funds so projects can be implemented sooner. In addition, each barangay nationwide will receive P200,000 from the Presidential Socio-Civic Projects Fund, amounting to more than P8 billion in direct support for development projects in communities. Recto said President Marcos has made clear that government support should increase when LGU programs are shown to work and deliver tangible benefits to communities. The LMP Mindanao Island Cluster Conference was also attended by Office of the Presidential Assistant for the Visayas (OPAV) Secretary Philip Lo, Cebu Province Governor Pamela Baricuatro, LMP National President Mayor Faustino “Inno” Dy V, LMP Vice President for the Mindanao Cluster Mayor Leonard Escobillo, and LMP-Cebu President Cesar Suan.

Marcos raises concern over social media's impact on children. President Marcos has raised concern over the growing influence of social media and online platforms on children, saying young people are increasingly exposed to harmful content and distorted realities while their critical judgment is still developing. Speaking at the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) Presidential Luncheon in Manila, Marcos said technology has become an integral part of daily life but also created risks for children who receive information and form opinions online. “As a parent, I am increasingly mindful of the influence of social media and online platforms on our children,” he said. Marcos said the government must balance technological innovation with greater responsibility to create a safer digital environment for young Filipinos. “Innovation must continue, certainly, but so must the responsibility that accompanies it,” he said. The President noted that the government is expanding digital literacy initiatives, modernizing cybersecurity initiatives, and promoting the holistic well-being of Filipinos while upholding freedom of expression. Disinformation, AI threats Marcos also warned that the rapid spread of false and manipulated information, including AI-generated content, is putting public trust under pressure. He said information, whether true or fabricated, can spread instantly through digital platforms, creating challenges not only for government but also for the media, business, academe, and civil society. The President stressed that credibility is particularly important for both government and journalists because it serves as the foundation of their work and the basis of public trust. He noted that the government has launched Oplan Kontra Fake News to protect the public from disinformation and hold its purveyors accountable. Press freedom pledge Meanwhile, President Marcos reiterated his commitment to protecting press freedom, saying the role of the President is to defend it rather than diminish it. “The Philippine government recognizes that a free, independent, and responsible press remains indispensable to any democratic society,” he said. He said media practitioners, including photojournalists, are government partners in promoting good governance and transparency. Stronger response to fake news President Marcos said the government is also strengthening mechanisms to protect journalists and respond to threats in the digital environment. Through the Presidential Task Force on Media Security, he said the government continues to strengthen legal assistance, coordination, and cybercrime response mechanisms to better protect media practitioners. He said the government and the media may not always agree, but their shared interest should remain the pursuit of truth. “The government and the media may not always agree, nor should they,” Marcos said, adding that both sides share an interest in ensuring that facts prevail over speculation and fake news.

After ten years, Instagram updates its logo with a modern look, and some users are not happy. Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, revealed a new logo last week. This is the first update for the content-sharing app in a decade. “The wordmark at the top of the app hasn’t changed in ten years, so it was time for a refresh,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri said in a post on the platform. “Cleaner and more modern, with references to the original and the simplicity and craft that’s always made it Instagram,” Mosseri said. Comments to the post pointed out that the “s” looked like a “z”. User @paulodelvalle commented: “Instagzam?” While user @thelosttwo raised issues Instagram is facing and said a new logo was prioritized over them. “Instead of fixing the algorithm, this is what you’re paying your employees 6 figures to do.” @masonversluis, who has 187 thousand followers, commented on the post: “Fixing broken things, but meanwhile your AI moderation has THOUSANDS of people WRONGFULLY banned, including my wife and a 12-year-old's account! FOCUS ON WHAT MATTERS.” Have you seen the new logo? What are your thoughts? Are you missing the old one?

Lala strengthens into a hurricane and bears down on Hawaii's Big Island with heavy rain, winds. Hawaii's Big Island was threatened Saturday with its first possible direct hit from a hurricane in 155 years as Hurricane Lala roared in the Pacific Ocean and gusty wind, waves and rain pounded the region. The National Hurricane Center said Lala's maximum sustained winds increased to 75 mph (120 kph), making it a Category 1 hurricane. The storm's center was forecast to move over or near the island's southern end by the evening, lashing its worst winds at volcanic slopes thousands of feet above sea level. Whitecap surf slammed ashore nonstop, howling winds whipped the tops of palm trees, and waterways swelled with fast-moving runoff from relentless rain that blew nearly sideways. Gov. Josh Green, noting rainfall of 2 inches (5 centimeters) an hour, said "people should be sheltering in place now." Forecasters said higher elevations on the island, dominated by the towering Mauna Kea volcano, could get as much as 25 inches (63.5 centimeters) of rain. That could cause life-threatening mudslides in a mountainous area where people live off the grid in improvised housing. Earlier the governor called it an "enormous storm," capable of destructive flooding and even the possibility of wildfires kicked up by strong winds across the island chain. Electricity was knocked out for 32% of customers on the Big Island, according to poweroutage.us. The island, population 210,000, is Hawaii's largest. Residents prepare for the worst Bobby Camara, a 75-year-old lifelong resident, said he planned to "hunker down, cross my fingers, hope the lights don't go out" at a care home just outside Hilo. He said gas stations were busy as people sought fuel for chain saws and vehicles. "I think stocking up is part of life over here. ... You learn to be self-reliant," Camara said. Mike Caputo, who lives in Keaau, near the Big Island's east coast, said his power generator was ready and a 10,000-gallon (37.8 kiloliter) home water tank was full. He said the main concern was flash flooding and fallen trees, especially albizia, a common tree. "They're not very sturdy, but they grow extremely large," said Caputo, 50, a local fire captain. "They can make roads impassable." Warnings posted everywhere The Big Island was under a hurricane warning, and tropical storm warnings were issued for the islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau. A Category 3 hurricane hit the northeast corner of the Big Island in 1871, according to research by a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist. The latest forecast has Lala striking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," said Vanessa Almanza, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Honolulu. Shelters were opened, events were canceled and ranchers were urged to leave their cattle in pastures, rather than structures that might collapse. "It doesn't take landfall to create destruction," Almanza said. Indeed, Christine Matsuda, who lives in Waimea, on the northern side of the island, said "big gusts every few minutes rattle the whole house." "We're finding unexpected leaks in places that don't see water under normal conditions," Matsuda said. The hurricane center predicted 8 to 12 inches (20.3 to 30.5 centimeters) of total rainfall across Maui and the lower elevations of the Big Island, and 4 to 6 inches (10.2 to 15.2 centimeters) across the island chain. Many Hawaii residents are still dealing with the aftermath of devastating floods in March. Wildfire risks increase during windy weather As winds ramped up across the islands, Almanza said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would elevate fire concerns. In 2023 the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south. "Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa of Lahaina, who is known in the area for his surfing, paddling and other ocean skills. Kauai, which is several islands northwest up the archipelago from the Big Island, is where Hurricane Iniki made landfall as a Category 4 hurricane in 1992 — an El Nino year like this one, when a warming of the Pacific near the equator increases Pacific hurricane activity and affects weather patterns across the globe. "It did $3 billion worth of damage. It destroyed thousands of homes, and it did kill six people," said Steven Businger, a University of Hawaii scientist. "We just can never know if a storm is going to turn."

Iran claims Qatar is holding pilots, Israeli strikes kill 11 in Lebanon, and other Middle East news. Iran said Qatar was holding three of its pilots who had been missing since March, which Qatar denied. The United Arab Emirates accused Iran of again attacking one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. The Iran-backed Houthis again struck a Red Sea port in Yemen. And in southern Lebanon, 11 people were killed in Israeli airstrikes, some of the deadliest since a shaky truce between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah went into effect on June 20. Here's a look at the latest developments on Saturday in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here. Iran says Qatar is holding 3 of its pilots Qatar's armed forces captured and were holding three pilots who went missing in March when their jets were downed, the Missing Persons Committee of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff said. Qatar, however, denied it. Until now, Tehran had said it had no information about their fate. This is the first known case in the war where Iran has said a regional country is holding its fighters. Qatar on March 2 said its air force shot down two Iranian bombers as Tehran lashed out against countries hosting U.S. military bases in the opening days of the war. Saturday's statement alleged that Qatar had not allowed the pilots to meet or communicate with families or Iranian officials handling their cases. Iran asked the International Committee of the Red Cross president for help. The letter said a fourth pilot was killed while on the mission "targeting an enemy military base in Qatar," state media reported. A spokesperson with Qatar's foreign ministry, Majed Al Ansari, later denied the claims and indicated on X that the pilots had been shot down and that Qatar's search and rescue teams found the remains of one. He said Iran was invited in April to visit and be briefed on those efforts, with no response. A tanker is attacked in the Strait of Hormuz The tanker owned by Abu Dhabi's state-owned oil and gas company ADNOC was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the Emirati state-run WAM news agency said Saturday. There were no injuries in the Friday evening attack, the agency reported. It was the third such attack on a vessel operated by ADNOC in the critical waterway in the last week. The United Arab Emirates in a statement called on Iran to stop the unprovoked strikes. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said a bulk carrier was struck in the hull by an unknown projectile on Friday. It was not immediately clear if it was the same vessel. Iran asserted control over the strait after the war started on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes. About one-fifth of the world's traded oil and natural gas passed through the waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf before then. Talks between the U.S. and Iran have stalled while Iran is in discussions with Oman about how to manage the strait that runs between them and had been considered an international waterway. Israeli strikes kill 11 in southern Lebanon Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people Saturday. Lebanon's Health Ministry and state news agency said one strike targeted a home on the edge of the village of Ansar and killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two. The second, on the village of Deir al-Zahrani, killed four and wounded 17. Israel's military said it killed a Hezbollah battalion commander and several other militants at a headquarters in southern Lebanon in response to the group's actions against Israeli soldiers operating there. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office in a separate statement said three soldiers were seriously injured. The military blamed an explosive drone. The military said the commander's family was with him, and that "it should be emphasized that the family members were not the target of the strike." Both the military and Netanyahu's office alleged the commander used the family members as human shields. It was one of the deadliest days since the Lebanese government and Israel announced a "framework agreement" laying out a plan for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for Hezbollah's disarmament. The militant group refused direct talks and was not part of the agreement. Houthis in Yemen attack Red Sea port, killing at least 3 Yemen's military said the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port of Mokha under the control of the internationally recognized government. Port director Abdul-Malik al-Sharabi told journalists that Friday evening's attack killed three people including two marines, and that port operations had been suspended. Military spokesperson Col. Majed al-Nazili said in a statement that the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles. The Houthis' attack was the latest on government-held areas and on neighboring Saudi Arabia, part of an escalation threatening to plunge Yemen back into civil war. Analysts say the escalation reflects how Iran is scaling up pressure on the United States and its regional allies.

Bedbugs can cause people to lose sleep — and blood. Here's what to do about them. NEW YORK (AP) — Bedbugs are sometimes called the vampires of the insect world — hiding during the day and coming out at night to feast on human blood. Generations of children have been told: "Sleep tight. Don't let the bedbugs bite." Well, bad news: Bedbug infestations are increasing. This is the time of year when they tend to be at their worst. And some scientists think the reviled pests might be capable of spreading an antibiotic-resistant infection called MRSA. For centuries, the bugs have horrified homeowners and occasionally panicked the public. That happened in New York City in 2018, when at least a half dozen city buses were taken out of service after reports of bedbugs crawling on seats. It happened again in Paris in 2023, when reports of bedbugs at a movie theater, on trains and on buses popped up in the lead-up to the 2024 Olympics. "They certainly are out there," said Christopher Hayes, a North Carolina State University assistant professor who has been bitten by bedbugs more than 50 times in the course of research. "And if you're unaware, if you're not on top of your game, it's easy to bring them into your home." Bedbugs really do come out at night Bedbugs are reddish-brown bloodsuckers about the size of an apple seed. Some researchers estimate they date back to the time of the dinosaurs, but they are best known for their unfortunate ability to live with — and prey on — humans. They can hide in narrow crevices in furniture and lurk in clothes, linens and mattresses. They are hard to see but can be detected through the small dark excrement stains they leave. The pests can be year-round problems but they have traditionally thrived in the summer. They tend to emerge at night, crawling onto people and using a beaklike body part to pierce human skin and suck blood for several minutes. The bite itself is painless. Some people develop itchy red welts a day or so later, but others have no reaction. That's a problem, because people unaware that they are repeatedly being bitten can quickly find themselves victims of an infestation. One of the more gruesome stories about bedbugs and human health was detailed in a 2020 medical journal case report from France. It told of a 70-year-old man who lived by himself in an apartment and fainted on the street one day. He was brought to a hospital emergency department in a Paris suburb where he was diagnosed with dementia — and with anemia caused by a longstanding loss of blood. He also had bedbugs feeding on his neck, head and shoulder. An investigation of his apartment detected thousands of them in his bed and on the floor, walls and curtains of his home. They aren't thought to spread disease, but one experiment raises questions Some good news about bedbugs is there hasn't been clear evidence that they have spread diseases from one person to another. The bugs' digestion and anatomy seem to prevent germs from being passed on efficiently, said Chow-Yang Lee, an entomologist at the University of California at Riverside. But University of South Dakota researchers in 2023 published the results of an experiment — using blood capsules with an artificial skin — that demonstrated bedbugs could acquire MRSA during one feeding and spread it during a later one. Follow-up research is needed to really prove bedbugs actually are spreading MRSA to people, said one of the study's authors, Jose Pietri, who is now at Purdue University. But "it changes the perspective of what bedbugs do, in terms of public health," Pietri said. Bedbugs are more resistant to pesticides Bedbug populations in developed countries were decimated after World War II due to the widespread use of the pesticide DDT. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency banned the pesticide for most uses in 1972, citing evidence that it was harming animals and was a potential risk to people. Bedbugs had already started to develop resistance to DDT by then, and they have only been getting stronger and more common, said Lee, noting that insecticide resistance has driven a continued resurgence in bedbugs in recent decades. Exactly how much more common isn't clear. Pest control companies generate annual rankings of U.S. cities with the worst bedbug problems. (Orkin currently ranks Chicago at No. 1, while Terminix says Philadelphia has the biggest problem.) But those lists are based on how many calls each company receives in a year, not a rigorous survey. Many bedbug infestations happen in low-income or public housing, which may not hire the big companies that compile those rankings, Lee said in an email. How to protect yourself from the pests The best thing you can do is never get them in the first place, experts say. That means not bringing them into your home. Travelers can pick them up in hotel rooms. So before you unpack for your stay, check the room for signs of bedbugs by pulling back the covers and bedsheets to look for bugs or fecal spots. Do not place luggage on beds or on the floor near beds, and consider placing your bags in a light-colored trash bag or even in the bathtub. When you get home, open the luggage outside and take laundry right to the washing machine and dryer. Sometimes, bedbugs enter homes by hitching a ride on secondhand furniture or other products. Visually inspect those items and treat them before you take them into your home, Hayes advised. Some experts advise vacuuming, steaming or heating furniture, and quarantining it in a garage or storage unit for a few days before bringing it inside the house. If it's clothes, wash them and put them through the dryer for an hour. Shoes or other items? Consider putting them in a freezer for a week "to make sure that everything in there that could be alive is taken care of," Hayes said. How to get rid of bedbugs if you have them The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency offers do-it-yourself guidance for getting rid of the pests, but it's labor-intensive, involving sealing hiding spaces and treating infested items. It also contains many warnings of what not to do. "You can't just blast random chemicals and expect it's going to work because there's a fairly high likelihood that they'll be resistant to some of the first-line insecticides," Pietri said. It makes sense to hire professional exterminators who are experienced in getting rid of bedbugs, Pietri and other experts said. But it can cost hundreds or even thousands of dollars. Insecticides are not the only option. Silica dust treatments, for example, absorb the bedbug's body moisture, killing them. Sustained dry heating works wonders, killing eggs as well as adult bedbugs. But it has to be at least 122 degrees (50 degrees Celsius) and can damage furniture, paintings and other personal possessions, so it must be done by professionals. "I think the biggest piece of advice is just people shouldn't panic," Hayes said. "They just need to take action. If you think you have bedbugs, don't wait to deal with it."

San Juan dumps Imus, secures top 4 in playoffs. The San Juan Knights toyed with the Imus Yangkees, 120-77, on Saturday, Aug. 15, to secure a top-four finish in the SportsPlus MPBL (Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League) 2026 Season round-robin elimination phase at the Pasay Astrodome. With all 15 Knights, headed by James Kwekuteye, scoring, San Juan led as far as 102-51 in securing its 17th win against two losses and tightening its grip of the second spot behind Abra Solid North (19-1) in the North division of the 26-team tournament. The top four finishers will have the homecourt advantage in the quarterfinal playoffs. Kwekuteye celebrated his 28th birthday by scoring 44 points, spiked with 7 triples, 3 assists and 2 rebounds, followed by Patrick Sleat with 13 points, 3 rebounds and 3 assists, and Harold Alarcon, with 12 points, 11 rebounds, 5 assists and 4 steals. The 6-foot-2 Kwekuteye, a former star of the San Beda Red Lions, was chosen the SportsPlus best player after leading the Knights to their third straight lopsided win after losing to the Quezon Huskers, 71-78, on July 30. "T was injured a month ago, and now I'm here (best player)," said Kwekuteye. Other Knights who shone were Reyland Torres with 12 points, 3 assists and 3 rebounds, and Michael Calisaan with 10 points, 4 rebounds and 3 assists. With Kwekuteye pumping in 12 points, the Knights surged ahead, 53-29, at halftime and never let up to pull Imus down to 3-17. Imus drew 20 points from Ian Pardo, 17 from Harold Lomlong, and 12 from homegrown Patrick Dale Beltran. The tournament visits the Malolos Convention Center on Monday, featuring games between Zamboanga and Manila at 3 p.m., Cebu and Meycauayan at 5 p.m., and Gensan and Bulacan at 7 p.m.

Novak Djokovic ousted from Cincinnati Open in his first match since Wimbledon. MASON, Ohio (AP) — Novak Djokovic's stay at the Cincinnati Open was a short one. It also might be his last. The 24-time major champion fell to Thiago Agustin Tirante 2-6, 6-4, 6-4 on Saturday, Aug. 15, in a match that took 2 hours, 44 minutes in hot and humid conditions. A 25-year-old from Argentina, Tirante is ranked No. 50 in the world. Djokovic — a three-time Cincinnati champion and No. 5 in the rankings — was playing for the first time since his loss to top-ranked Jannik Sinner in the semifinals at Wimbledon. Up next for Djokovic is the U.S. Open, which starts Aug. 30 in New York. Djokovic appeared to struggle physically in the heat and had his 10-match winning streak in Cincinnati snapped. The 39-year-old told reporters that an unspecified health condition made it difficult for him to play in hot and humid weather. “It’s just a condition that I have, health-wise, that has been bothering me for the past couple of years,” Djokovic said. “A lot of issues, especially when it is humid and it is hot. I did anticipate it (would be humid), but there are all these things, like nerves and everything involved that make it worse, and that’s what happened.” Djokovic has had plenty of success in Cincinnati, with a 45-13 record and titles in 2018, 2020 and 2023. But he wasn't sure he would return. “I certainly hope so, but it looks more likely not, unfortunately,” Djokovic said. “But let’s see what the future brings.” Djokovic saved 13 of the 15 break points he faced. Tirante broke Djokovic's serve in the ninth game of the final set and then served it out. “I think this is the best win of my career,” Tirante said. “I think I really did a good job inside the court. I managed very well the nerves of playing against a legend like Novak.”

Scheffler holds 2-shot lead in Memphis. MEMPHIS, Tenn. (AP) — Scottie Scheffler settled in after a rough start Saturday, Aug. 15, for a 2-under 68, giving him a two-shot lead over Sam Burns and Sungjae Im in the FedEx St. Jude Championship going into a final round where so much is at stake from the top to the bottom of the leaderboard. Scheffler is trying to break a streak of five runner-up finishes and five other top 4s since his lone victory this year in his first tournament of 2026. He was at 13-under 197 and will be in the final group with Burns, his closest friend in golf, who got back into the mix with a 62. His year has been marked by close calls in the U.S. Open and British Open, but Burns has no victories to show for it. This will be the first time they are paired together in the final group. “It's always a little weird just because I want him to have success so much and I think he wants the same for me,” Scheffler said. "Tomorrow we'll go out there and play our game and see where things finish up at the end of the day. It will be competition like normal. “It will be fun being out there with your friend but it’s also a bit weird at the same time.” And it's not just the two of them. Im shot 67 and was tied with Burns at 11-under 199. The next closest to Scheffler was FedEx Cup champion Tommy Fleetwood (68) and Jake Knapp (67), both five shots behind. Jordan Spieth took another step back and gave himself another Sunday at the TPC Southwind filled with high stress. Spieth is at No. 54 in the FedEx Cup, and only the top 50 advance to the BMW Championship next week in the FedEx Cup playoffs. The top 50 is the magic number this week because those players are assured to getting into all the $20 million signature events next year. Spieth, who opened with a 65, didn't make a birdie until the 11th hole in his round of 72 that dropped him from a tie for fifth to a tie for 19th, which is projected to leave him out of the top 50. He's not alone. Brian Harman came in at No. 65 and shot 69. He was in a tie for sixth, needing to move up a few spots to advance. “That signature series, it's where you want to be,” Harman said. “It's where the best golf is played.
